title: FIN13
summary: FIN13, also tracked as Elephant Beetle, is a financially motivated intrusion set that public reporting describes as active since at least 2016 and focused on financial services, retail, and payment processing organisations, with much of the documented activity in Latin America and the United States. Its defining characteristic is patience and coverage rather than speed. Operators have been reported to maintain access for months or years, mapping payment related systems and internal applications, and to abuse publicly accessible services, weak remote access, and known vulnerabilities in internet facing middleware to gain entry. Persistence and movement rely heavily on built-in administration features, scheduled jobs, database services, and legitimate remote management tools, which makes their activity resemble routine maintenance. The goal is card data and the ability to move money, so the systems worth watching are payment switches, transaction databases, and anything that touches cardholder data. Long dwell time means log retention and baseline knowledge of normal administrative behaviour matter more than any single indicator.

beginner.definition: FIN13, also called Elephant Beetle, is the name for a group that steals money and payment card information. Public reports say it has been active since at least 2016. It targets banks, shops, and payment companies, mainly in Latin America and the United States. It is a criminal group that wants profit, not political secrets. Its main skill is patience.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group does not smash and grab. It moves in quietly and stays for a long time, learning how your payment systems work before it takes anything. Servers that face the internet are its usual way in, especially when updates are delayed. Because it uses normal administration tools, its activity looks like a colleague doing maintenance. If your logs are kept for only a few weeks, you may never see how it arrived. You cannot fix a door you cannot find.
howItWorks: The attackers scan for internet facing systems such as web servers and payment applications.
They get in using a known flaw, a weak password, or a remote access service left open.
They create their own accounts and scheduled jobs so they can return after a reboot.
They map which servers process transactions and where card data is stored.
They move between systems using built in administration tools that rarely raise alarms.
They copy transaction data and move money slowly, often over many months.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop where the back office door is always unlocked because staff only use the front. Someone slips in, sits at the empty desk, and quietly learns the alarm codes and the safe combination. He even restocks a shelf so the manager thinks he works there. Weeks later he empties the safe. FIN13 works this way, because nobody treats a person doing normal office tasks as a threat.
takeaways: Patch internet facing systems quickly, since that is how this kind of group usually gets in.
Keep logs for many months, because long hidden intrusions are invisible in short records.
Know which servers touch payment data and watch who logs into them.

objectives: Explain why dwell time makes log retention a critical defensive control.
Describe how internet facing applications become an entry path for financially motivated actors.
Identify the persistence mechanisms an intruder creates to survive restarts and password changes.
Explain why administrative tools blend in and how baselining helps you spot misuse.
Map the systems in a payment environment that warrant the closest monitoring.
Outline a review process for dormant or unnecessary services exposed to the internet.
